title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
author: Mary Wollstonecraft
openingText:
Sir,

Having read with great pleasure the pamphlet on national education that you recently published, I dedicate this volume to you — the first dedication I have ever written — in order to induce you to read it attentively; and I do so because I think you will understand me, which I do not expect of the many impertinent little wits who may ridicule the arguments they cannot answer. But, sir, my respect for your understanding goes further still: so far that I am confident you will not toss my work aside and hastily conclude that I am wrong merely because you did not see the subject in the same light yourself. And forgive my frankness, but I must remark that you treated it too superficially, content to regard it as it had been regarded in the past, when the rights of man, to say nothing of woman, were trampled on as a fantasy. I therefore call on you now to weigh what I have put forward concerning the rights of woman and national education; and I call with the firm voice of humanity. For my arguments, sir, are dictated by a disinterested spirit: I plead for my sex, not for myself. I have long considered independence the great blessing of life, the basis of every virtue; and I will always secure my independence by reducing my needs, even if I had to live on a barren heath.
about:
Mary Wollstonecraft examines how education, economic dependence and social expectations shape women’s lives. She attacks the ideal that teaches women to please rather than think independently, and argues for education, independent judgment and shared moral standards for women and men.

Published in 1792, the book connects domestic life with politics and justice. Wollstonecraft discusses Rousseau’s views on women, marriage, modesty, parental responsibilities and schooling for girls and boys together. She argues that oppression damages both those made dependent and those who exercise power over them.

angleCards.title: Education and independence
angleCards.text: Follow her argument that what women learn and are permitted to do shapes their abilities and choices.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how Wollstonecraft connects education with women’s independence.

angleCards.title: The argument with Rousseau
angleCards.text: Wollstonecraft quotes and challenges Rousseau’s view that women’s education should serve men’s needs.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow her objections to Rousseau’s account of women and education.

angleCards.title: One moral standard
angleCards.text: The book insists that virtue rests on reason and applies to women and men alike.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the case for shared moral standards and its application to marriage and modesty.

angleCards.title: Home and society
angleCards.text: Family life, work, rank and political rights become parts of the same discussion.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how inequality at home connects with inequality in society.

cast.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
cast.description: She addresses the reader directly, tests her arguments against everyday life and criticizes both male power and women’s learned habits.

cast.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
cast.description: His account of women’s education in Emile is quoted and challenged, particularly in chapter 5.

cast.name: Reason
cast.description: The faculty that Wollstonecraft believes must develop if a person is to act independently and morally.

cast.name: Talleyrand
cast.description: The French politician and former bishop whose writing on national education provides the dedication’s starting point. She asks him to apply principles of freedom and rights to women.

cast.name: The accomplished woman
cast.description: The woman trained in social accomplishments and attractiveness without the development of independent judgment.

whyItMatters.title: Rights and responsibilities
whyItMatters.body: Wollstonecraft links rights with the capacity to fulfil duties. A person denied freedom to exercise reason cannot also be expected to act morally from independent conviction.

whyItMatters.title: Education is political
whyItMatters.body: Schooling and upbringing shape more than individuals. They affect marriage, parenthood, economic dependence and social power.

whyItMatters.title: An argument to examine
whyItMatters.body: The book combines radical demands for freedom with period assumptions about gender, religion and society. Readers can follow its arguments closely while examining where those assumptions limit them.
